item.title: “One who finds no core among becomings, Like one picking flowers from a fig tree — That monk abandons the near and far shore, Like…
item.description:
“One who finds no core among becomings,
Like one picking flowers from a fig tree —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

“One in whom there is no anger inside,
Who has gone beyond existence and non-existence —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

“One whose thoughts have been dispersed,
Internally well-ordered, without remainder —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 1.1

item.title: “One who restrains evil intent, Seeing the beautiful with sharp desire — That person’s craving increases; He makes the fetter strong.” “One who delights in…
item.description:
“One who restrains evil intent,
Seeing the beautiful with sharp desire —
That person’s craving increases;
He makes the fetter strong.”

“One who delights in calming the mind,
Always contemplating foulness, mindful —
That person will destroy craving;
He cuts off Māra’s fetter.”

“One who has reached the goal, without fear,
Free from craving, without defilement,
Having pulled out the dart of existence —
This body is his last.”

From: Dhammapada 334-359

item.title: Greed, hatred, delusion — these three, Are evil minds for a person, They damage one’s own self, They produce one’s own self, Like the rind…
item.description:
Greed, hatred, delusion — these three,
Are evil minds for a person,
They damage one’s own self,
They produce one’s own self,
Like the rind and core of a tree,
Producing its own fruit.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.2
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, sensual thought is blind, causes blindness, causes lack of knowledge, leads to the destruction of wisdom, partakes of distress, does not lead to Nibbāna.…
item.description:
“Monks, sensual thought is blind, causes blindness, causes lack of knowledge, leads to the destruction of wisdom, partakes of distress, does not lead to Nibbāna. Monks, ill-will thought is blind … harmful thought is blind, causes blindness, causes lack of knowledge, leads to the destruction of wisdom, partakes of distress, does not lead to Nibbāna.

Three thoughts of wholesome kind
One should frequently reflect upon —
Three unwholesome thoughts should be abandoned, turned away from.
That one surely restrains
The conduct of thoughts.

As rain settles the dust,
So by calming thoughts with the mind,
One here and now attains
The peaceful path of peace.”

From: Itivuttaka 87

item.title: “Rāhula, develop the meditation on foulness. Rāhula, by developing the meditation on foulness, what is called lust is abandoned. Rāhula, develop the meditation on impermanence.…
item.description:
“Rāhula, develop the meditation on foulness. Rāhula, by developing the meditation on foulness, what is called lust is abandoned. Rāhula, develop the meditation on impermanence. Rāhula, by developing the meditation on impermanence, what is called the conceit ‘I am’ is abandoned.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 62 – Mahārāhulovādasutta

item.title: “Monks, I will teach about suffering and the root of suffering. Listen … And what, monks, is suffering? Form, monks, is suffering; feeling is suffering;…
item.description:
“Monks, I will teach about suffering and the root of suffering. Listen … And what, monks, is suffering? Form, monks, is suffering; feeling is suffering; perception is suffering; formations are suffering; consciousness is suffering. This, monks, is called suffering. And what, monks, is the root of suffering? It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there — that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.31
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And what, monks, is the peril in the case of feelings? Feelings are impermanent, suffering, subject to change – that is the peril in the…
item.description:
“And what, monks, is the peril in the case of feelings? Feelings are impermanent, suffering, subject to change – that is the peril in the case of feelings. And what, monks, is the escape in the case of feelings? The removal of desire and lust for feelings, the abandoning of desire and lust – that is the escape in the case of feelings.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 13 – Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta

item.title: “And how, householder, is wandering without a home? Regarding the form element, householder, whatever there is of desire, lust, delight, craving, any engagement and clinging,…
item.description:
“And how, householder, is wandering without a home? Regarding the form element, householder, whatever there is of desire, lust, delight, craving, any engagement and clinging, mental standpoints, attachments, underlying tendencies — the Tathāgata has abandoned them, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, made them non-existent, so that they cannot arise again in the future. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called ‘one who wanders without a home.’ Regarding the feeling element … perception element … formation element … consciousness element — the Tathāgata has abandoned them … Therefore, the Tathāgata is called ‘one who wanders without a home.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.3
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, what is Right Effort? Monks, here a monk awakens desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy,…
item.description:
“Monks, what is Right Effort? Monks, here a monk awakens desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. He awakens desire for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. He awakens desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. He awakens desire for the continuance, non-disappearance, strengthening, increase, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. This, monks, is called Right Effort.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 22 – Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta

item.title: “And for what benefit, monks, should a monk dwell with the perception of disgust toward the non-disgusting? ‘May greed not arise in me toward agreeable…
item.description:
“And for what benefit, monks, should a monk dwell with the perception of disgust toward the non-disgusting? ‘May greed not arise in me toward agreeable states.’ For this benefit, monks, a monk should dwell with the perception of disgust toward the non-disgusting. And for what benefit, monks, should a monk dwell with the perception of non-disgust toward the disgusting? ‘May hatred not arise in me toward states that provoke hatred.’ For this benefit, a monk should dwell with the perception of non-disgust toward the disgusting. And for what benefit should a monk, abandoning both the non-disgusting and the disgusting, dwell equanimously, mindful and clearly comprehending? ‘May greed not arise in me toward agreeable states, wherever, however; may hatred not arise in me toward states that provoke hatred, wherever, however; may delusion not arise in me toward states that provoke delusion, wherever, however.’ For this benefit, monks, a monk, abandoning both the non-disgusting and the disgusting, dwells equanimously, mindful and clearly comprehending.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.144
